newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: U.S group says IRA violence undermines support.
newsitem.headline: U.S group says IRA violence undermines support.

text.p: An influential U.S. figure in the Northern Ireland peace process said on Thursday that the Irish Republican Army's return to violence after a 17-month truce had humilated American supporters of their cause.

"Those who violated the faith of the people in America and their friends, who embarrassed us and humiliated us, are going to find out that the price to be paid for that is enormous," Bill Flynn, chairman of the National Committee on American Foreign Policy, told a Dublin news conference.
"It is the violence we detest not the principles for which they (the IRA) are fighting for," Flynn said. The IRA wants to end British rule of the province.
"Their principles should not be achieved over dead bodies," Flynn said after talks with all parties in the Northern Ireland conflict on both sides of the border.

"Violence leads nowhere except to further violence," said Flynn, whose group successfully lobbied for the granting of a U.S. visa to Gerry Adams, president of the IRA's political wing Sinn Fein, in 1994.

Flynn was commenting on the IRA's ending of a 17-month ceasefire in February with a London bomb blast followed last week by an attack on a British army base in Northern Ireland in which one soldier died.
Sinn Fein is excluded from Belfast peace talks until it restores its ceasefire, the British and Irish governments say.

"I am here to make known to the parties involved how Americans feel, of their condemnation of the violence and to tell them that there will never be peace unless all sides return to negotiation," Flynn said.

Flynn, who will take the results of his fact-finding visit back to U.S. President Bill Clinton, said he had faith in Adams, who has been shunned by the British and Irish governments because of the ending of the truce.

"I simply trust this man, and others trust him. And I believe he is going to play a key role in peaceful resolution. Without him, I see no peaceful resolution. I cannot associate him with the violence," Flynn said.
He said Adams could not condemn IRA violence because it would weaken his leadership of the Irish Republican movement.
"If he were to reject what was being done violently, he would no longer be a force of leadership. I have no doubt he rejects entirely the violence approach," Flynn said.
"Violence does not solve the problem in Northern Ireland, peace negotiations do," Flynn said.
